clue.text: Buffet snack served with wicked lunch (not cold)

indicators.note: served up in a new form, so the letters of the dish are dished out again in another order
the bracketed 'not' says a letter is dropped from the word lunch

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone at a buffet picks up a snack to go with a rather naughty lunch, minus anything cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' looks like a spread of food but is a verb or noun for a blow. Drop C from LUNCH to get LUNH, then 'served' shuffles SNACK, WICKED and LUNH together.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffet is a blow, and a punch in the mouth is slang known as a knuckle sandwich.

clue.text: Sex symbol of 10 — can king arise, tired?

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upwards, so the pieces are written in reverse order

parts.note: Bo Derek became a sex symbol after starring in the 1979 film 10
taken as written
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A question about a film sex symbol and whether a weary king can get up.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to 10 across, but it is the film title. 'arise' turns DEREK CAN K upwards. KNACKERED is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Knackered is informal British slang meaning utterly exhausted or worn out, a synonym for tired.

clue.text: Feminine new piece's ugly, not good on the exterior

indicators.note: the trimmed word sits on the outside, wrapping round the other pieces
not good tells us to remove the abbreviation for good

parts.note: taken as written
a man is a piece in chess or draughts

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a new feminine work as ugly and poorly finished on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piece' is a chess or draughts man, not a work of art; 'not good' trims ugly, and the remainder wraps the new piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Something considered unmanly lacks masculine qualities, so it can loosely be called womanly or feminine.

clue.text: Atonement had her sounding gallant

indicators.note: sounding signals that we want a word that is pronounced like the name, not spelt like it

parts.note: Keira Knightley starred in the 2007 film Atonement

explanation.surface: A remark that a film featured a particular actress who sounded noble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Atonement' is not repentance here but the film of Ian McEwan's novel, which starred Keira Knightley.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaving like a knight means being chivalrous and courteous, which is what gallant means.

clue.text: Softened exams: education department primarily welcomes top grades

indicators.note: welcomes means the first letters take in the next piece, holding it inside
primarily means we take the first letters of the three words before it

parts.note: A is the top exam grade, so two of them are AS

explanation.surface: Exams were made easier as the education department lets in more top grades.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials of 'exams', 'education' and 'department' give EED, which takes in AS.
explanation.definitionFit: Eased means made less severe or harsh, the same as softened or lessened.

clue.text: A don, not working, prepares lectures

indicators.note: not working says to drop the word meaning in operation from the word don

parts.note: taken as written
on means working, as a machine that is on
to dress food or a wound is to prepare it

explanation.surface: A university don who is not at work gets ready to give lectures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don' looks like the lecturer but is just letters: remove ON to leave D.
explanation.definitionFit: To address an audience is to speak formally to it, so addresses and lectures are both verbs for speech-making.

clue.text: Introductory line for explorer in TV guide: "Mostly old Inspector Morse reruns"

indicators.note: reruns suggests something run again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged
mostly means almost all of the word old, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A TV listings magazine notes that the old detective series Inspector Morse is mostly repeats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link but is part of the fodder: IN, TVGUIDE, OL and INSPECTORMORSE are rearranged by 'reruns'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley's greeting on finding the missing explorer in Africa in 1871 is the famous opening remark of their meeting.

clue.text: Breaks in Irish rugby union squad's first tackling exercise

indicators.note: tackling means grappling with, so these letters clasp the next piece between them
first means just the opening letter of squad

parts.note: PT is physical training, a word for exercise

explanation.surface: An Irish rugby union squad begins a tackling drill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tackling' is a rugby word in the surface but here means gripping: the union abbreviation plus the squad's initial clasp the exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrupt is to burst or force one's way in suddenly, the same as breaking in.

clue.text: Cartoon character is a big hit in America

definitions.meaning: the father in The Simpsons, the cartoon family
in baseball a home run is a hit that clears the field

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure is said to be a big success in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'big hit' looks like popularity but is a baseball home run.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer Simpson is the cartoon dad, and a homer is American slang for a home run in baseball.

clue.text: Branch where motor mechanics change body parts

parts.note: an arm is a branch, as of a river or an organisation
in motor racing the mechanics change tyres in the pits

explanation.surface: A garage branch where mechanics swap out car parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body parts' sounds like car bodywork but means parts of the human body. The pits are the servicing area beside a racing track.
explanation.definitionFit: The hollows under the shoulders where arm meets torso are parts of the human body.

clue.text: Good behaviour last month, no booze

parts.note: December, abbreviated DEC, is the last month of the year
O stands for nought or nothing, so for no
rum is an alcoholic drink, booze

explanation.surface: Someone behaved well last month by going without alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorum is propriety and seemly conduct, which is good behaviour in polite company.

clue.text: Know Clarke (or Clark cut short)?

indicators.note: cut short means the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Clark Kent is the everyday identity of Superman

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking whether you know Clarke, or a Clark trimmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clarke' points to Ken Clarke, a long-serving British Conservative politician; the bracket gives a second route via Clark Kent losing his T.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken is a Scottish and archaic verb meaning to know or be aware of something.

clue.text: Low flyer's landing spot to limit helicopter? Not initially

parts.note: a helipad is marked with a large letter H showing where to land
an edge is a limit or boundary

indicators.note: not initially means the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a chopper is a slang word for a helicopter

explanation.surface: A low-flying pilot needs a landing pad to keep the helicopter in check.
explanation.walkthrough: The landing spot is the big letter painted on a helipad; 'Not initially' trims the slang word for helicopter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedgehopper is a pilot or plane that flies very close to the ground, a low flyer.

clue.text: Grand with wealthy player's unbeatable hand?

parts.note: royal can mean grand or splendid
flush means having plenty of money

explanation.surface: A rich card player holding a grand hand that cannot be beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the ace-high straight in a single suit is the best possible hand and cannot be beaten.

clue.text: Hurry! Ladies getting trade round back of park

indicators.note: round means these letters go around the next piece

parts.note: the ladies is a British name for women's toilets, loos

indicators.note: back of means the last letter of the word park

parts.note: a mart is a market, a place of trade

explanation.surface: Women rush to do business around the far end of a park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ladies' is the British name for a women's public toilet; the plural of the everyday British word for toilet wraps the end of park.
explanation.definitionFit: Look smart is a British idiom ordering someone to be quick, so it means hurry up.

clue.text: Exploited the Guardian journalist

parts.note: this puzzle appears in the Guardian, which refers to itself as us
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A complaint that the newspaper's reporter was taken advantage of.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian setting a puzzle speaks as 'us'.
explanation.definitionFit: To use someone is to take selfish advantage of them, so used means exploited.

clue.text: Pass on time — no hospital to standards for nutritional study

parts.note: to pass on is a euphemism for to die

indicators.note: no means the following letter is taken out of the next word

parts.note: ethics are moral standards
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Instructions to move a deadline with no hospital in mind, for a food-science course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass on' looks like handing something over but means to die. ETHICS without H gives ETICS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dietetics is the science of diet and nourishment, the study of nutrition.

clue.text: See 6
Doctor with tablet turning head of Michael Barrymore?

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

indicators.note: turning here means turning a letter upside down, so an M becomes a W
head of means the first letter of Michael

explanation.surface: A doctor gives a pill to the TV presenter Michael Barrymore.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Barrymore was a British TV entertainer; the definition is just 'Barrymore?', pointing to the actress Drew Barrymore. Turning M upside down gives W.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark shows the definition is by example: the actress Drew is one Barrymore.

clue.text: Ring banks of Everton, mid-range club?

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its two edges, so we take the outer letters of Everton

parts.note: a five iron, V IRON with V the Roman numeral five, is a mid-range golf club

explanation.surface: A question about whether Everton is a mid-table football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' looks like football (Everton is a Liverpool football club) but is a golf club, the five iron.
explanation.definitionFit: To environ is to surround or encircle, so it is a verb meaning to ring.

clue.text: Something blown well: blower gets behind America

indicators.note: gets behind means this piece is placed after the one before it

parts.note: so and well are both interjections opening a remark
USA is America
the blower is old British slang for the telephone

explanation.surface: Someone blowing well gets behind a patriotic American band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blower' looks like a musician, but it is slang for the phone.
explanation.definitionFit: The sousaphone is a large brass tuba-like instrument played by blowing, so it is something blown.

clue.text: Independent and i hold up small supplement — men at the top make paper work

indicators.note: at the top means this piece goes first in a down answer

parts.note: OR are other ranks, ordinary soldiers or men

indicators.note: hold means the two letters grip the next piece between them

parts.note: taken as written, a single letter

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a mag is a short word for a magazine, a newspaper supplement

explanation.surface: Two newspapers, the Independent and the i, delay a small magazine while senior men make the paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper work' is split from 'paperwork': it means art made of paper. The i is a British newspaper, so both papers give a single letter; 'up' turns the supplement.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes, so its products are works of paper.

clue.text: Partners and opponent, three times holding unknown hand, might catch this?

parts.note: in bridge South and North are partners, S and N

indicators.note: holding means the repeated letters grip the next piece

parts.note: East is an opponent of North-South at bridge, E, here taken three times
Z is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: A bridge scene where partners and an opponent hold an unknown hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand' looks like the cards dealt, but it is the hand you catch a sneeze in. S and N, the bridge partners, then EEE around Z.
explanation.definitionFit: When you sneeze you may cover your mouth and catch the spray in your hand.

clue.text: See 6
Cut down one chapter to make deduction

parts.note: to log is to cut down trees
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An editor trims a chapter to make a cut or reduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deduction' looks like a subtraction but means reasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is reasoning from premises to conclusions, the process of deduction.

clue.text: Top three characters for United in scoreless draw

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the zeroes of the score

parts.note: a nil-nil draw is written 0-0, two Os
UTD is the three-letter abbreviation for United in football results

explanation.surface: United's top three players feature in a goalless draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective but is a verb meaning beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo someone is to surpass or beat them, which is what to top them means.

clue.text: Short, firm president

indicators.note: short means the company's name is cut by its last letter

parts.note: IKEA is the Swedish furniture firm

explanation.surface: A description of a small, determined head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short, firm' looks like a description of the president but means a firm's name cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Ike was the nickname of Dwight Eisenhower, the 34th US president.

clue.text: Starts to get excited — Ronnie's back, eyeing reds and making plant

indicators.note: starts to means we take the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Snooker fans get excited as Ronnie O'Sullivan returns, lining up the red balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie O'Sullivan is a famous English snooker player, and reds are the red balls in snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: The gerbera is a daisy-like flowering plant from southern Africa, grown for its bright flowers.

clue.text: Fish nets close to whales mark one disturbance at sea

indicators.note: nets means the fish catches the following letter inside it

parts.note: tuna is a fish

indicators.note: close to means the last letter of whales

parts.note: M is short for mark, the old German currency
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fishing boat nets a fish near whales, marking one disturbance at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea wave set off by an earthquake, a great disturbance of the ocean.

clue.text: Sweet products in set, refine Coco Pops

indicators.note: pops suggests things bursting and scattering, so the letters before it jump into a new order

explanation.surface: A breakfast cereal brand's chocolate puffs set the standard for refined sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: Coco Pops is a chocolate breakfast cereal; here 'Pops' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Confectioneries are sweets and candies, the goods made and sold by a confectioner.
